Find the statement that is false.
(1) True — erythromycin binds the bacterial ribosome and stops protein synthesis without killing
the cell, so it is bacteriostatic.
(2) True — ampicillin is semi-synthetic. Natural penicillin G is chemically modified to broaden
its spectrum, so it is not a natural antibiotic.
(4) True — vancomycin acts on a wide range of organisms, so it is broad spectrum.
(3) False — prontosil **is** converted into sulphanilamide in the body. Prontosil itself is
inactive in the test tube; it is a prodrug, reduced by enzymes in the body to release
sulphanilamide, which is the active antibacterial.
That discovery was historically important: it showed a drug could be activated by metabolism,
and sulphanilamide became the parent of the whole sulpha drug family.
∴ statement (3) is not true.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|53||0|0.s:
Work backwards from the product, o-bromobenzoic acid.
KMnO₄/OH⁻ oxidises a side chain –CH₃ to –COOH, so R must be o-bromotoluene.
The step before used NaNO₂/HCl at 273–278 K followed by H₃PO₂. That is diazotisation, then
reduction with hypophosphorous acid, which replaces the –N₂⁺ group by –H. So Q carried an
–NH₂ that has been removed altogether, and Q was 2-bromo-4-aminotoluene.
Before that, Sn/HCl reduced –NO₂ to –NH₂, so the amino group was originally a nitro group.
So P is a nitrotoluene, brominated in the first step.
Now check which one gives bromine in the right place. Take p-nitrotoluene, with CH₃ at C1 and
NO₂ at C4. The CH₃ directs ortho and para; the NO₂ directs meta. Position 2 is ortho to CH₃
and meta to NO₂, so both directors point there and the bromine enters at C2 ✓
That places Br ortho to the methyl, which becomes the COOH — exactly the product shown.
The amino group is used only to block and then removed, a classic directing-group strategy.
∴ P is p-nitrotoluene.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|54||0|0.s:
Two steps.
Acetic acid with calcium hydroxide is simply neutralisation, giving the calcium salt:
2CH₃COOH + Ca(OH)₂ ⇒ (CH₃COO)₂Ca + 2H₂O
Dry distillation of the calcium salt of a carboxylic acid gives a ketone and calcium carbonate:
(CH₃COO)₂Ca ⇒ CH₃COCH₃ + CaCO₃
The two methyl groups end up joined through the carbonyl, so the product is propanone (acetone).
This is a general method: the calcium salt of any acid RCOOH gives the symmetrical ketone RCOR.
Note what it does *not* give — an aldehyde. Ethanal would require a mixed calcium salt with
formate, (HCOO)(CH₃COO)Ca.
∴ propanone.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|55||0|0.s:
Boron in BX₃ has only six valence electrons and an empty 2p orbital, so all the halides are
Lewis acids. The question is which is strongest, and the answer is counter-intuitive.
On electronegativity alone fluorine should pull hardest and make BF₃ the best acceptor. But
back bonding overrides that.
The filled 2p orbital on fluorine is the same size as boron's empty 2p, so the sideways overlap
is excellent and electron density is donated back into boron's empty orbital. This is pπ–pπ
back bonding, and it is **maximum in BF₃**.
That back donation partly fills the orbital the Lewis acid needs for accepting a lone pair, so
BF₃ is the **weakest** Lewis acid of the series.
Going down the group the halogen p orbital grows larger and more diffuse, overlap with boron's
2p worsens, back bonding falls away, and acidity rises:
BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃ < BI₃
So (1) and (2) are both the wrong way round, and (4) contradicts the overlap argument.
∴ there is maximum pπ–pπ back bonding in BF₃.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|56||0|0:
Bond dissociation energy of a C–H bond is governed by the stability of the radical left behind —
the more stable the radical, the less energy needed to make it.
Toluene has a benzylic C–H, on the CH₃ attached to the ring. Breaking it gives the benzyl
radical, C₆H₅CH₂•, and the unpaired electron is delocalised into the ring over three further
positions. That extensive resonance makes it the most stable radical here, so the bond is the
weakest, around 368 kJ mol⁻¹.
n-Pentane offers secondary C–H bonds, giving a secondary radical stabilised only by weak
hyperconjugation — about 410 kJ mol⁻¹.
2,2-Dimethylpropane has only primary C–H bonds, giving the least stable radical of the alkanes.
Benzene is worst of all: its C–H is on an sp² carbon, the radical formed lies in the plane of the
ring and cannot overlap the π system at all, so no resonance stabilisation is available — about
473 kJ mol⁻¹.
This is exactly why toluene is halogenated at the side chain under free radical conditions.
∴ toluene.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|57||0|0.s:
H₂S is a weak acid and ionises only slightly:
H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻
Adding HCl floods the solution with H⁺. By Le Chatelier, that common ion pushes the
equilibrium to the left and suppresses the ionisation, so the concentration of S²⁻ is kept very low.
Whether a sulphide precipitates depends on whether the ionic product exceeds its Ksp:
[M²⁺][S²⁻] > Ksp
Group 2 cations (Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺) form sulphides with extremely small Ksp, so even this tiny
[S²⁻] is enough to exceed it and they precipitate.
Group 4 cations (Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺, Co²⁺, Ni²⁺) form sulphides with much larger Ksp, so the low
[S²⁻] is not enough and they stay in solution.
That is the whole point of acidifying before passing H₂S — it separates the two groups. Group 4
is then precipitated by making the solution ammoniacal, which raises [S²⁻] again.
∴ because of the lower concentration of S²⁻.
